title: AIM-HIM: Governed Architecture and Evaluation Protocol for AI-Assisted Member Identity Resolution in Cross-Payer Healthcare Systems
content: Background: Cross-payer member identity resolution is foundational to healthcare interoperability and a persistent barrier to coordinated care. Duplicate and fragmented member records impair care coordination, administrative efficiency, and population health analytics across Medicaid, Medicare, and commercial payer environments. The growing adoption of Payer-to-Payer data exchange under CMS-0057-F and the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA) intensifies the need for governed, auditable member identity architectures. Objective: To specify AIM-HIM, a governed master data management architecture for healthcare member identity resolution and golden-record creation, and assess selected components through synthetic proof-of-concept experiments. Methods: The five-layer design combines ingestion, standardization, identity resolution, attribute survivorship, and governance. The architecture reflects patterns researched and implemented during professional practice as a Data Architect and Analyst (2017–2024), with AI enhancement since 2024. A linkage experiment used 1,200 synthetic persons with 480 held-out identities; a separate survivorship experiment evaluated 24,000 attribute decisions across five simulation seeds. Results: The hybrid matcher achieved precision 0.998, recall 0.944, and F1 0.970. Ungated logistic regression achieved F1 0.976; the hybrid's lower recall reflects a deliberate design tradeoff—routing DOB-contradictory pairs to human stewardship rather than automatic acceptance—at the cost of recall in this synthetic scenario. Confidence-weighted survivorship achieved 97.02% accuracy versus 89.50% and 92.11% for two fixed-priority baselines, conditional on correct identity links and an informative simulated quality signal. Discussion: The experiments illustrate component feasibility under simplified assumptions. Conclusion: AIM-HIM provides a testable architecture and evaluation protocol. Independent replication, stronger baselines, realistic benchmarks, and authorized real-world validation will further strengthen the evidence base.
